item.text:
Yes—unequivocally. Sotalol is a known hERG/Kv11.1 (IKr) blocker; this is its intended Vaughan–Williams class III activity, but it also creates a clinically established QT-prolongation and torsades de pointes liability. The current US label carries a boxed warning for life-threatening proarrhythmia. At 160–640 mg/day, mean QTc increases are approximately 10–40 ms and are dose/exposure related. [DailyMed prescribing information](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=d6c8f659-1c32-4431-bdb2-3211a1c81006)

What I would tell the team:

- Treat sotalol as a clinically validated torsadogenic positive comparator—not merely a compound with a theoretical hERG flag.
- It is a relatively low-affinity, assay-sensitive hERG blocker: reported potency ranges from hundreds of micromolar to millimolar depending on temperature, expression system, pulse protocol and equilibration. Block is state/use dependent; one study found substantial block only after repetitive depolarization and prolonged exposure. A short or low-concentration screen can therefore under-call it. [Mechanistic hERG study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11090546/)
- Consequently, sotalol is an excellent translational comparator for APD/MEA, in-vivo QT and exposure–QT studies, but a less convenient sole positive control for routine hERG assay performance. I would also include a high-affinity control such as dofetilide or E-4031.
- Interpret comparisons using unbound exposure and full concentration–response data. Sotalol is essentially unbound, not metabolized, and renally eliminated unchanged; renal impairment can markedly increase exposure.
- In vivo, separate direct IKr effects from its nonselective β-blockade. Bradycardia can both complicate QT correction and amplify torsadogenic risk.
- Key risk multipliers are high dose/exposure, reduced creatinine clearance, slow heart rate, female sex, heart failure, baseline long QT, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia and concomitant QT-prolonging drugs. The label requires ECG/electrolyte/renal-function monitoring during initiation and dose escalation.

One metadata point: the supplied SMILES leaves the stereocentre unspecified. Marketed sotalol is the racemate; both enantiomers have similar class III activity, whereas β-blockade resides mainly in the l-enantiomer. I would record the exact stereochemical form and salt used in the comparator study.
